title: The cosmic paradox of Anish Kapoor
gist: A studio-and-gallery profile of Anish Kapoor at 72, in what the critic calls his biggest year — Hayward return, Palazzo Manfrin, US and Finland shows, a photography book — built around the paradox that Britain's most politically outspoken artist insists his work has no message. The critic argues Kapoor's anti-biographical stance sets him against a London art market currently monetising artist-as-subject, and concludes his work is strongest outside the gallery frame.

themes.theme: The outspoken artist who says nothing

insights.claim: Anish Kapoor's public positions are unusually confrontational for a blue-chip artist: he threatened to sue after US border agents posed in front of Cloud Gate in Chicago, called for the US to be excluded from the Venice Biennale alongside Israel and Russia, staged a guerrilla Greenpeace artwork on a North Sea gas platform, and described Narendra Modi's India as a “Hindu Taliban” and a “fascist regime”.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Political exposure of this magnitude is now compatible with top-tier institutional and collector demand — a change in what the art market tolerates.
insights.locator: He has threatened to sue after United States border agents

insights.claim: Kapoor's most unwavering credo, held consistently from a 1998 conversation with Homi K Bhabha to today, is that he has nothing particular to say and no message to give anyone.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: A 28-year-consistent artistic position, which makes the political/artistic separation a genuine structure rather than a defensive line.
insights.quote: I’ve got nothing particular to say, I don’t have a message to give anyone
insights.locator: So it might seem strange, at least at first

insights.claim: Kapoor distinguishes bringing something to expression from being expressive, arguing that entrenched ego has many ways of taking over what the artistic message can be.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: A transferable creative-process rule: the maker as conduit rather than subject, which is the opposite of the personal-brand model dominating contemporary culture.
insights.quote: I think it’s my role as an artist to bring to expression, it’s not my role to be expressive.
insights.locator: There are so many ways that entrenched ego attempts

insights.claim: Believing it is everyone's duty to have at least some kind of political agenda, Kapoor has signed open letters against genocide in Gaza and against the introduction of ID cards in Britain, and handed journalists stickers for an anti-far-right march organised by the Together Alliance.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Maps the specific UK political causes drawing elite cultural backing — ID cards and anti-far-right organising.
insights.locator: He has signed open letters against genocide in Gaza

insights.claim: The tension between opposing forces is not incidental to Kapoor's work but its point: material versus immaterial, visceral versus sterile, religious versus secular, and even what is and is not art.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Gives a working criterion for judging any Kapoor piece — does it sustain contradiction, or resolve into one side.
insights.locator: What is more unusual is that it is this display of apparent paradox

insights.claim: The prevailing experience Kapoor aims at is uncertainty arising from contradiction — a “strange in-betweenness, between nothingness and eternal possibility” that the viewer must discover for themselves.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Explains why his work resists interpretation-driven marketing, which is both its critical strength and a commercial friction.
insights.quote: It’s in that strange in-betweenness, between nothingness and eternal possibility, that the viewer has to discover for themselves.
insights.locator: Whether it’s in one of his meaty works

insights.claim: Kapoor invokes Barnett Newman's principle that scale is not a matter of size but a matter of meaning, a distinction the critic then turns back on Kapoor's own career: the size of his success may not carry the heft of scale to warrant it.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: A reusable test separating volume of output and exposure from genuine significance — applicable to any asset where scale is mistaken for substance.
insights.quote: Barnett Newman used to say that scale is not a matter of size
insights.locator: But as Kapoor himself might argue

insights.claim: Kapoor rejects both the universalist and the purely visceral readings of his work: asked whether he is tapping something universal he fires back “Universal for whom?”, while insisting the bodily reactions his blood-and-guts sculptures provoke are partly incidental and partly carefully worked at.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Closes off the two easiest critical frames, which is why his work stays hard to price interpretively.
insights.quote: I like the idea of eliciting reactions that are beyond words, where you tumble into feeling a sensation, something that you don’t quite know how to describe
insights.locator: An easy answer might be that Kapoor is trying to tap

insights.claim: The test Kapoor applies to art is whether a personal story can transcend into mythological or historical recall, and when pressed on how to judge that, he falls back on “It's really a matter of quality”.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: The criterion is circular at the decisive point — an honest limit on connoisseurship as a valuation method.
insights.quote: Does it just relate to my little story, or can my little story transcend and become something else?
insights.locator: What resources do we have as human beings?

insights.claim: Kapoor's Hayward show stands against the other major London exhibitions of the summer — Tracey Emin at Tate Modern, Frida Kahlo's self-portraiture, and Marilyn Monroe portraits at the National Portrait Gallery — all of which trade on artist-as-sitter and on real people and real lives.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Identifies the dominant programming strategy of major UK institutions — biography sells — and the one blue-chip artist refusing it.
insights.locator: And on this point alone Kapoor’s Hayward show is conspicuous

insights.claim: Kapoor argues museums all over the world are obsessed with where an artist comes from, concedes the correction may have been overdue, but insists the real question is whether the object holds any poetic value.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: A senior non-white artist pushing back on identity-led curation — a signal that the curatorial pendulum may be nearing its limit.
insights.quote: Museums all over the world are obsessed with where an artist comes from
insights.locator: “Museums all over the world are obsessed

insights.claim: Kapoor's own position shifted: in a 1983 BBC interview with William Feaver he described his work as a rediscovery of how to be Indian, a framing he has since abandoned — plausibly because his biography, born in India to a Punjabi Hindu father and Iraqi-Jewish mother who fled Baghdad, educated at the Doon School and a spell on an Israeli kibbutz, defies easy categories.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Shows the anti-identity stance is biographically produced rather than ideological — relevant to how his work will be historicised.
insights.locator: It should be said that Kapoor was not always so eager

insights.claim: Absent autobiographical handrails, viewers are forced into a more interrogative posture — what is this, how am I supposed to look at it, what is it meant to mean — because the appeal of a human story is precisely how easily it can be parsed within the mirror of our own lives.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Explains the commercial advantage of biography-led shows: parseability drives attendance, which is why institutions favour it.
insights.locator: In any case, one thing that makes Kapoor’s work

insights.claim: The clinical quality critics complain about — a consequence of rubber, steel and silicone and technically complex fabrication — is better read as deliberate impersonality, since Kapoor is concerned with formal arrangements first and wants viewers thinking about nobody at all.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Reframes the standard critical objection as design intent, which matters for how the work is assessed long-term.
insights.quote: I’m going to tell you about my little story?
insights.locator: One of the most common criticisms levelled at his work

insights.claim: Kapoor returned to the Hayward Gallery in June for the first time since his career-defining 1998 show, alongside the Palazzo Manfrin in Venice opening only for the second time ever, a US paintings exhibition, a show in Finland and a photography book — the most simultaneous public access to his work there has ever been.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Peak institutional saturation for a living artist typically coincides with peak market attention — a marker for his primary and secondary pricing.
insights.locator: Without doubt, this is Kapoor’s year.

insights.claim: All of Nothing (2026), a giant red inflatable filling the Hayward's first gallery and bulging between concrete columns upstairs, is judged the perfect execution of Kapoor's paradox — making the room feel at once larger than possible and smaller than it appears.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: The critic's clearest endorsement in the show; simple concept plus technical difficulty is the formula that works.
insights.locator: As you walk into the Hayward

insights.claim: Ha Makom, the show's crowning piece — a massive red spider-like mound with a roughcast cenotaph, titled with the Hebrew for “the place” and referencing God's immanence — is judged not to transcend, because it is neutered by the Hayward's white walls as a decontextualised object plucked from its natural habitat.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: The headline work fails on the critic's own transcendence test — the central negative verdict of the review.
insights.locator: On the top floor of the Hayward sits what might be

insights.claim: The same Ha Makom haunted the critic in Kapoor's studio months earlier, unfinished and worked on by assistants in respirator masks and plastic overalls who looked as if they were excavating a dead alien exoskeleton — evidence the work is most powerful encountered without wall texts, titles or press releases.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Argues presentation context can destroy value in the encounter — a real consideration for how monumental work is sited and sold.
insights.locator: I think back to how it haunted me

insights.claim: Vantablack, the coating that absorbs virtually all light and flattens three-dimensional surfaces, anchors one gallery, including a recreation of Descent into Limbo — the 2.5m-deep hole made infamous in 2018 when a man in Portugal mistook it for a carpet and fell in — now hemmed in by wires.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Illustrates how a material patent and a viral accident became durable brand assets for an artist.
insights.locator: Next is a room of works made in Vantablack

themes.theme: Studio, control and the next projects

insights.claim: At the Palazzo Manfrin, with its vast partially derelict interior and a semi-abstract pamphlet offering minimal explanation, Kapoor operates in his natural provisional in-between space, where visitors arrive as acolytes and fellow travellers — including Korean sculptor Lee Ufan wandering in to say hello.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Artist-controlled foundations function as reputational infrastructure distinct from museums and dealers.
insights.locator: With its vast and still partially derelict interior

insights.claim: Kapoor's studio operates as a closed fortress: an assistant approached for comment on what it is like to work there declined in accordance with Kapoor's wishes, so there is no penetrating beyond what Kapoor wants you to see.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Tight information control around a major studio practice — relevant to how much outside parties can actually verify about production and output.
insights.locator: When I approach one of his assistants

insights.claim: Painting is the part of the practice Kapoor holds most precious because it is the one he controls completely — unlike sculptures requiring teams of assistants over months, he always paints alone, accompanied only by a statue of the Buddha.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Total authorial control is the scarce good in a studio system built on delegated fabrication — a distinction that can matter for attribution and value.
insights.locator: But despite this clear turn towards increasingly quixotic projects

insights.claim: Kapoor has a serious proposal to launch an artwork into outer space that would be visible from Earth, and a concept for a deep fleshy scar cutting across the entire length of Great Britain that he calls a playful attempt at commentary.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Signals where monumental public art ambition is heading next — orbital and landscape scale, with the attendant regulatory and planning obstacles.
insights.quote: What’s interesting is the idea of an object of whatever kind sitting in cosmic dimensions
insights.locator: Another equally ambitious idea

insights.claim: Kapoor defines the artist's role through Pollock: taking paint he thinks of as blood and seed, pouring it repeatedly in a kind of mad frenzy, then putting it on the wall where it stops being blood and seed and becomes cosmic — “fundamental, alchemical transformation”.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: The clearest statement of Kapoor's value theory: repetitive material labour converted into meaning by context and framing.
insights.quote: That’s the artist’s role in the end, isn’t it? Fundamental, alchemical transformation.
insights.locator: “What does Pollock do?” Kapoor asks.

insights.claim: The critic's final verdict is that “transformation” is too final a word for what Kapoor does and “mediation” fits better: he has built a model universe with its own internal logic but insists we explore it without playing by its rules, which is why even his unconvincing work is never not engaging.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: The reviewer's settled judgement — durable engagement rather than consistent success, which is a defensible position for a long-career artist.
insights.locator: Except “transformation” isn’t quite the right word

insights.claim: At the Manfrin opening an opera singer lay on the floor to sing into the maw of At the Edge of the World, a giant bell-like sculpture that absorbs sound, animating the void until a ringing phone broke the illusion — the critic's example of Kapoor's work succeeding through something the artist did not control.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
entities: At the Edge of the World
insights.so_what: The strongest recorded effect came from an unplanned collaboration, underlining that the work depends on encounter rather than object.
insights.locator: There is an event to celebrate the opening of the Manfrin
